newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan leader to visit unspecified Latam countries.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan leader to visit unspecified Latam countries.

text.p: Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui will make side trips to unspecified third countries during a September visit to Panama despite rival China's moves to sabotage his journey, senior officials said on Monday.
"The president's Central American trip is likely to include two to three nations, but no final plans have been made yet," foreign minister John Chang told a parliament meeting.
"A number of Carribean nations have also hoped that President Lee can visit them on his way," Chang said. "President Lee is likely to visit a friendly country in the Carribean."
Panama has invited Lee to attend a September 7-10 conference on the future of the Panama Canal -- affording him a rare chance to meet U.S. President Bill Clinton and other world leaders.
Taiwan reportedly donated US$800,000 to help organise the conference marking 20 years since adoption of a U.S.-Panamanian treaty ceding full control of the canal to Panama in 1999.
Communist China, which has viewed Taiwan as a renegade province since a civil war split them in 1949, has pressured Panama to rescind Lee's invitation.
Panama, one of just 30 countries that recognise the exiled Republic of China on Taiwan rather than Beijing's communist People's Republic, has declined.
Chang said China had set up an ad-hoc committee to deal with Panama's invitation for Lee and stepped up pressure on Panama.
"The pressure is rather heavy and the Chinese communists are doing all they can to stop President Lee from visiting (Panama)," Chang said.
Chang said the committee has worked hard to try to undermine Taiwan-Panama diplomatic ties.
Chang said his ministry was confident ties would remain unchanged despite Beijing's squeeze.
Taiwan's biggest ally, South Africa, announced in November that it would switch recognition to Beijing in 1997.

In more than four decades of rivalry with Taiwan, Beijing has urged the world to drop diplomatic ties with Taiwan, saying the Nationalist-ruled island, as a mere province of China, had no right international recognition.
Chang pledged to work hard to counter Chinese moves in denying Taiwan's existence in international community.
